claim: Identifying cell names in dense image stacks is critical in analyzing functional whole-brain data enabling comparison across experiments.
source: Although identifying cell names in dense image stacks is critical in analyzing functional whole-brain data enabling comparison across experiments, unbiased identification is very difficult, and relies heavily on researchers' experiences.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a motivation for the work, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Unbiased identification of cell names in dense image stacks is very difficult and relies heavily on researchers' experiences.
source: Although identifying cell names in dense image stacks is critical in analyzing functional whole-brain data enabling comparison across experiments, unbiased identification is very difficult, and relies heavily on researchers' experiences.
evidence: This is stated as a problem in the abstract, representing knowledge about current limitations.

claim: CRF_ID is a probabilistic-graphical-model framework based on Conditional Random Fields for unbiased and automated cell identification.
source: Here, we present a probabilistic-graphical-model framework, CRF_ID, based on Conditional Random Fields, for unbiased and automated cell identification.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the nature of the presented method.

claim: CRF_ID focuses on maximizing intrinsic similarity between shapes.
source: CRF_ID focuses on maximizing intrinsic similarity between shapes.
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of the method in the abstract.

claim: CRF_ID achieves higher accuracy on simulated and ground-truth experimental datasets compared to existing methods.
source: Compared to existing methods, CRF_ID achieves higher accuracy on simulated and ground-truth experimental datasets, and better robustness against challenging noise conditions common in experimental data.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental comparisons shown in the manuscript.

claim: CRF_ID shows better robustness against challenging noise conditions common in experimental data compared to existing methods.
source: Compared to existing methods, CRF_ID achieves higher accuracy on simulated and ground-truth experimental datasets, and better robustness against challenging noise conditions common in experimental data.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing performance under various noise conditions.

claim: CRF_ID can boost accuracy by building atlases from annotated data in a highly computationally efficient manner.
source: CRF_ID can further boost accuracy by building atlases from annotated data in highly computationally efficient manner, and by easily adding new features (e.g. from new strains).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the data-driven atlas building methodology described in the manuscript.

claim: CRF_ID can easily add new features from new strains to boost accuracy.
source: CRF_ID can further boost accuracy by building atlases from annotated data in highly computationally efficient manner, and by easily adding new features (e.g. from new strains).
evidence: This is demonstrated by incorporating landmark cells and spectral information in the model.

claim: The authors demonstrate cell annotation in Caenorhabditis elegans images across strains, animal orientations, and tasks including gene-expression localization, multi-cellular and whole-brain functional imaging experiments.
source: We demonstrate cell annotation in Caenorhabditis elegans images across strains, animal orientations, and tasks including gene-expression localization, multi-cellular and whole-brain functional imaging experiments.
evidence: This is supported by the various experimental demonstrations presented in the results section.

claim: Annotation of anatomical structures at cellular resolution in large image sets is a common data analysis step in many studies in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Annotation of anatomical structures at cellular resolution in large image sets is a common data analysis step in many studies in Caenorhabditis elegans such as gene expression pattern analysis (Long et al., 2009; Murray, 2008), lineage tracing (Bao et al., 2006), multi-cell calcium imaging and whole-brain imaging (Schrödel et al., 2013; Kato et al., 2015; Venkatachalam et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in the field.

claim: Cell annotation is necessary for cellular resolution comparison of data across animals, trials, and experimental conditions.
source: It is necessary for cellular resolution comparison of data across animals, trials, and experimental conditions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the importance of cell annotation.

claim: In whole-brain functional imaging, meaningful interpretation of population activity critically depends on cell identities as they facilitate the incorporation of existing knowledge about the system.
source: Particularly in whole-brain functional imaging, meaningful interpretation of population activity critically depends on cell identities as they facilitate the incorporation of existing knowledge about the system (Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Cell identities are needed for applying common statistical data analysis methods such as Principal Component Analysis, Tensor Component Analysis, demixed-Principal Component Analysis.
source: Cell identities are also needed for applying common statistical data analysis methods such as Principal Component Analysis, Tensor Component Analysis, demixed-Principal Component Analysis (Williams et al., 2018; Kobak et al., 2016) etc as data across experiments needs to be indexed and pooled by cell identities before applying these methods.
evidence: This is supported by citations to methods papers.

claim: The use of cell-specific markers as landmarks delivers good accuracy but has the cost of having to engineer cell-specific reagents without interfering with phenotypes of interest, which is not guaranteed.
source: Typically, the use of cell-specific markers as landmarks delivers good accuracy, but has the cost of having to engineer cell-specific reagents without interfering with phenotypes of interest, which is not guaranteed.
evidence: This represents knowledge about current methods and their limitations.

claim: Even with markers such as the NeuroPAL collection, there is still a need to automate the cell identification process.
source: Further, even with markers such as the recently developed impressive reagents in the NeuroPAL collection (Yemini et al., 2021), there is still a need to automate the cell identification process.
evidence: This is stated as motivation for the work, with citation to NeuroPAL.

claim: In the absence of markers, cells are identified by comparing images to a reference atlas such as WormAtlas and OpenWorm atlas.
source: In the absence of markers, cells are identified by comparing images to a reference atlas such as WormAtlas (Altun and Hall, 2009) and OpenWorm (Szigeti et al., 2014) atlas.
evidence: This describes current practice with citations to atlas resources.

claim: Reference atlases assume a static and often single view of the anatomy.
source: Reference atlases assume a static and often single view of the anatomy; in contrast, anatomical features vary across individuals.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of reference atlases.

claim: Anatomical features vary across individuals.
source: Reference atlases assume a static and often single view of the anatomy; in contrast, anatomical features vary across individuals.
evidence: This represents established biological knowledge.

claim: Due to variations in experimental conditions during acquisition, image data often do not match the static atlases, making manual cell identification extremely difficult if not infeasible.
source: Moreover, due to variations in experimental conditions during acquisition such as exact resolution and orientation of animals, image data often do not match the static atlases, making manual cell identification extremely difficult if not infeasible.
evidence: This describes a practical challenge based on experimental observations.

claim: Position noise is caused by individual-to-individual variability in cell positions compared to positions in atlas.
source: First, individual-to-individual variability in cell positions compared to positions in atlas (position noise).
evidence: This defines a type of noise observed in data.

claim: Count noise is caused by mismatch between number of cells in image and atlas.
source: Second, mismatch between number of cells in image and atlas (count noise).
evidence: This defines another type of noise observed in data.

claim: Count noise is primarily caused by variability in the expression levels of the reporter used to label cells across animals, incomplete coverage of promoter to label desired cells, and limits in the computational methods to detect cells.
source: Count noise is primarily caused by variability in the expression levels of the reporter used to label cells across animals (i.e. mosaicism), incomplete coverage of promoter to label desired cells, and limits in the computational methods to detect cells.
evidence: This explains the sources of count noise based on experimental knowledge.

claim: In normalized coordinates, a cell's position can deviate from the atlas position by more than the cell's distance to its tenth nearest neighbor in the image.
source: Empirical data have shown that in normalized coordinates, a cell's position can deviate from the atlas position by more than the cell's distance to its tenth' nearest neighbor in the image (Yemini et al., 2021; Toyoshima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: 30–50% of cells in atlases may be missing from images.
source: Further, our data, as well as data from other labs, have shown that 30–50% of cells in atlases may be missing from images (Kato et al., 2015; Venkatachalam et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data from the authors and citations to other studies.

claim: As a result of large position and count noise common in data, identifying densely packed cells in head ganglion images of C. elegans by manually comparing images to the atlas is extremely difficult, even for experienced researchers.
source: As a result of the large position and count noise common in data, identifying densely packed cells in head ganglion images of C. elegans by manually comparing images to the atlas is extremely difficult, even for experienced researchers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the described noise levels.

claim: Manual annotation is labor intensive.
source: Further, manual annotation is labor intensive.
evidence: This is stated as common knowledge about manual methods.

claim: Previous computational methods for cell identification in C. elegans images focused on identifying sparsely distributed cells with stereotypical positions in young larvae animals.
source: Previous computational methods for cell identification in C. elegans images (Long et al., 2009; Long et al., 2008; Qu et al., 2011; Aerni et al., 2013) focused on identifying sparsely distributed cells with stereotypical positions in young larvae animals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous methods.

claim: Tools for identification of cells in whole-brain datasets, that is in dense head ganglion, do not exist.
source: Tools for identification of cells in whole-brain datasets, that is in dense head ganglion, do not exist.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in existing methods.

claim: Previous methods do not explicitly address the challenges imposed by the presence of position and count noise in the data.
source: Further, previous methods (Long et al., 2009; Yemini et al., 2021; Qu et al., 2011; Aerni et al., 2013; Toyoshima, 2019; Scholz, 2018) do not explicitly address the challenges imposed by the presence of position and count noise in the data.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous methods with citations.

claim: Previous methods maximize only extrinsic similarity between images and atlas, which is highly sensitive to count noise, position noise, and pre-alignment of spaces.
source: Thus, these methods maximize only extrinsic similarity (Bronstein et al., 2007) between images and atlas, which is highly sensitive to count noise, position noise, and pre-alignment of spaces in which the image and the atlas exist (i.e. orientations of animals in images and atlases).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous methods with citation to the concept of extrinsic similarity.

claim: With the amount of position and count noise commonly observed in experimental data, registration-based methods produce large matching errors.
source: With the amount of position and count noise commonly observed in experimental data, registration-based methods produce large matching errors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sensitivity of registration methods to noise.

claim: An alternative criterion proposed for topology-invariant matching of shapes is to maximize intrinsic similarity.
source: An alternative criterion proposed for topology-invariant matching of shapes is to maximize intrinsic similarity (Bronstein et al., 2007; Bronstein et al., 2009), orthogonal to extrinsic similarity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to shape matching literature.

claim: Intrinsic similarity has advantages because noise that affects extrinsic similarity does not necessarily imply worse intrinsic similarity.
source: This approach has advantages because noise that affects extrinsic similarity does not necessarily imply worse intrinsic similarity.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical advantage of intrinsic similarity.

claim: Although cell positions in an image may deviate from their positions in the atlas, geometrical relationships among them are largely maintained.
source: For instance, although cell positions in an image may deviate from their positions in the atlas (large extrinsic noise), geometrical relationships among them are largely maintained (low intrinsic noise).
evidence: This is stated as an example of the advantage of intrinsic similarity.

claim: Although absolute positions of the cell bodies of AIBL and RIML in an image may deviate greatly from their atlas positions, AIBL soma stays anterior to RIML soma.
source: As a specific example, although absolute positions of the cell bodies of AIBL and RIML in an image may deviate greatly from their atlas positions, AIBL soma stays anterior to RIML soma.
evidence: This is given as a specific example of preserved geometrical relationships.

claim: Intrinsic similarity is more robust against noises, independent of the pre-alignment of spaces, and inherently captures dependencies between cell label assignments that registration methods do not consider.
source: Therefore intrinsic similarity is more robust against noises, independent of the pre-alignment of spaces, and inherently captures dependencies between cell label assignments that registration methods do not consider.
evidence: This is stated as advantages of intrinsic similarity based on inference.

claim: The authors cast the cell annotation problem as a Structured Prediction Problem and build a Conditional Random Fields (CRF) model to solve it.
source: To directly optimize for intrinsic similarity and dependencies between label assignments, we cast the cell annotation problem as a Structured Prediction Problem (Bakir, 2007; Nowozin, 2010; Caelli and Caetano, 2005; Kappes et al., 2015) and build a Conditional Random Fields (CRF) model (Lafferty et al., 2001) to solve it.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach with citations.

claim: The CRF model directly optimizes cell-label dependencies by maximizing intrinsic and extrinsic similarities between images and atlases.
source: The model directly optimizes cell-label dependencies by maximizing intrinsic and extrinsic similarities between images and atlases.
evidence: This describes how the CRF model works.

claim: CRF_ID outperforms existing methods in handling both position noise and count noise common in experimental data across all challenging noise levels.
source: Further, CRF_ID outperforms existing methods in handling both position noise and count noise common in experimental data across all challenging noise levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental comparisons in the results.

claim: The authors took advantage of spatially distributed fluorescently labeled landmark cells to improve accuracy.
source: To further improve accuracy, we took two approaches. First, we took advantage of spatially distributed (fluorescently labeled) landmark cells.
evidence: This describes one approach to improve accuracy.

claim: Landmark cells act as additional constraints on the model, thus aiding in optimization, and helping in pre- as well post-prediction analysis.
source: These landmark cells act as additional constraints on the model, thus aiding in optimization, and helping in pre- as well post-prediction analysis.
evidence: This explains the role of landmark cells in the model.

claim: The authors developed a methodology to build data-driven atlases that capture the statistics of the experimentally observed data for better prediction.
source: Second, we developed a methodology to build data-driven atlases that capture the statistics of the experimentally observed data for better prediction.
evidence: This describes the second approach to improve accuracy.

claim: The annotation framework enabled the authors to analyze the simultaneously recorded response of C. elegans head ganglion to food stimulus and identify two distinct groups of cells whose activities correlated with distinct variables – food sensation and locomotion.
source: For the whole-brain imaging experiments, our annotation framework enabled us to analyze the simultaneously recorded response of C. elegans head ganglion to food stimulus and identify two distinct groups of cells whose activities correlated with distinct variables – food sensation and locomotion.
evidence: This is supported by the whole-brain imaging results presented.

claim: CRF is a graphical model-based framework widely used for structured/relational learning tasks in Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision community.
source: CRF is a graphical model-based framework widely used for structured/relational learning tasks in Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision community (Bakir, 2007; Nowozin, 2010; Lafferty et al., 2001; Sutton and McCallum, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to CRF literature.

claim: The problem is similar to structured labeling since the labels to be assigned to neurons are dependent on each other.
source: The problem is similar to structured labeling (Nowozin, 2010) since the labels to be assigned to neurons are dependent on each other.
evidence: This is stated with citation to structured labeling literature.

claim: If a certain neuron is assigned label AVAL, then the neurons that can be assigned label RMEL become restricted since only the cells anterior to AVAL can be assigned RMEL label.
source: For example, if a certain neuron is assigned label AVAL, then the neurons that can be assigned label RMEL become restricted since only the cells anterior to AVAL can be assigned RMEL label.
evidence: This is given as an example of label dependencies.

claim: Unary features account for extrinsic similarity and cell-specific features.
source: While unary features account for extrinsic similarity and cell-specific features, pairwise features account for intrinsic similarity.
evidence: This describes the role of unary features in the model.

claim: Pairwise features account for intrinsic similarity.
source: While unary features account for extrinsic similarity and cell-specific features, pairwise features account for intrinsic similarity.
evidence: This describes the role of pairwise features in the model.

claim: The authors encode pairwise dependencies between all pairs of cells in the form of several geometrical relationship features.
source: To maximize accuracy, we encode pairwise dependencies between all pairs of cells in the form of several geometrical relationship features (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the features used in the model.

claim: Optimizing the energy function over fully connected graphs is known to be an NP-hard problem.
source: Optimizing this energy function over fully connected graphs (more specifically graphs with loops) is known to be an NP-hard problem (Kohli et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with citation to computational complexity literature.

claim: Approximate inference algorithms are widely used in CRF community as they provide reasonable solutions.
source: However, approximate inference algorithms are widely used in CRF community as they provide reasonable solutions.
evidence: This represents knowledge about CRF methods.

claim: The authors implemented Loopy Belief Propagation to infer the most probable labeling over all cells, as well as marginal distributions of label assignments for each cell.
source: We implemented a popular method called Loopy Belief Propagation (Murphy et al., 1999) to infer the most probable labeling over all cells, as well as marginal distributions of label assignments for each cell.
evidence: This describes the optimization method used with citation.

claim: The features used in the base version of the model are geometrical relationship features that ensure identities assigned to cells in image are consistent with the atlas in terms of satisfying pairwise geometrical relationships.
source: The features used in the base version of the model are geometrical relationship features that ensure identities assigned to cells in image are consistent with the atlas in terms of satisfying pairwise geometrical relationships.
evidence: This describes the features in the base model.

claim: All geometrical relationship features are a variant of the quadratic Gromov-Wasserstein distance used in matching metric spaces and shapes.
source: All these features are a variant of the quadratic Gromov-Wasserstein distance used in matching metric spaces (Bronstein et al., 2009; Peyre et al., 2016) and shapes (Solomon et al., 2016; Mémoli, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to mathematical literature.

claim: The CRF model can be easily updated to include additional features such as cells with known identities and fluorescent spectral codes of cells.
source: We show that the CRF model can be easily updated to include additional features such as cells with known identities (landmark cells) and fluorescent spectral codes of cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by incorporating these features in the model.

claim: A critical component for the success of automated cell identification methods is data-driven atlas.
source: A critical component for the success of automated cell identification methods is data-driven atlas.
evidence: This is stated as an important finding.

claim: Static atlases such as OpenWorm atlas provide a single observation of positional relationships among cells.
source: Static atlases such as OpenWorm atlas provide a single observation of positional relationships among cells.
evidence: This describes a limitation of static atlases.

claim: Data-driven atlases relax the hard-coded constraint of 100% probability imposed by static atlas and accounts for the statistics that is observed experimentally for all positional relationship features.
source: Thus, data-driven atlases relax the hard-coded constraint of 100% probability imposed by static atlas and accounts for the statistics that is observed experimentally for all positional relationship features (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the advantage of data-driven atlases.

claim: Data-driven atlas built in the CRF_ID framework is considerably different from those built by registration-based methods.
source: Note, data-driven atlas built in our framework is considerably different from those built by registration-based methods.
evidence: This is stated as a distinction of the approach.

claim: Registration-based atlases store probabilistic positions of cells, while atlases built by CRF_ID framework store only probabilistic pairwise positional relationship features among cells.
source: While the latter atlases store probabilistic positions of cells, atlases built by our framework store only probabilistic pairwise positional relationship features among cells, thus more generalizable.
evidence: This describes the difference between atlas types.

claim: Building data-driven atlases is easy for the CRF model.
source: We show that building such data-driven atlases is easy for our CRF model (Appendix 1–Extended methods S1.7).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the methods.

claim: Building data-driven atlases is computationally cheap in CRF_ID, requiring only simple averaging operations.
source: Further, building data-driven atlases is computationally cheap in CRF_ID, requiring only simple averaging operations; thus, it is scalable to build atlases from large-scale annotated data that may become available in future.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method.

claim: 74% of cells were correctly identified by the top label prediction in the ground-truth data set using data-driven atlases.
source: With data-driven atlases (of only eight annotated set, one for each test dataset), 74% of cells were correctly identified by the top label prediction in the ground-truth data set, which exceeds the state of the art.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results on ground-truth data.

claim: 88% of cells had true identities within the top 3 predicted labels.
source: Further, 88% and 94% of cells had true identities within the top 3 and the top 5 predicted labels, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental results.

claim: 94% of cells had true identities within the top 5 predicted labels.
source: Further, 88% and 94% of cells had true identities within the top 3 and the top 5 predicted labels, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental results.

claim: Automated annotation is unbiased because the framework can combine manual annotations of cell identities of several users in the form of data-driven atlases.
source: More importantly, automated annotation is unbiased because, in principle, the framework can combine manual annotations of cell identities of several users (possibly across labs) in the form of data-driven atlases and can predict identities such that positional relationships in the atlas are maximally preserved.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage based on the method's design.

claim: Automated annotation removes individual biases in annotating cells.
source: Thus, automated annotation removes individual biases in annotating cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the unbiased nature of the method.

claim: The CRF_ID framework greatly supports researchers with no prior experience.
source: Further, it greatly supports researchers with no prior experience.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of the automated approach.

claim: Both position noise and count noise affect accuracy significantly.
source: We found that both position noise and count noise affect accuracy significantly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D) with position noise having a larger effect (compare scenarios 1–2 with 3–4 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by simulations on synthetic data.

claim: Position noise has a larger effect on accuracy than count noise.
source: We found that both position noise and count noise affect accuracy significantly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D) with position noise having a larger effect (compare scenarios 1–2 with 3–4 in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of scenarios in synthetic data.

claim: 10–15% improvement in prediction accuracy can be attained by simply improving reagents and eliminating count noise.
source: Results on both synthetic data and real data show that 10–15% improvement in prediction accuracy can be attained by simply improving reagents and eliminating count noise (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by results on synthetic and real data.

claim: Randomly chosen landmarks increased prediction accuracy by ~10–15%.
source: Indeed, we found, in both experimental data and synthetic data, randomly chosen landmarks increased prediction accuracy by ~10–15%.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with landmarks.

claim: The prediction results for experimental data lay close to the estimated bounds using synthetic data.
source: Notably, the prediction results for experimental data lay close to the estimated bounds using synthetic data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of experimental and synthetic results.

claim: Good agreement between results obtained on synthetic and experimental data suggest that the general trends uncovered using synthetic data of how various noises affect accuracy are applicable to experimental data.
source: Together, good agreement between results obtained on synthetic and experimental data suggest that the general trends uncovered using synthetic data of how various noises affect accuracy are applicable to experimental data.
evidence: This is an inference from the agreement between synthetic and experimental results.

claim: Among all co-dependent positional relationship features, the angular relationship feature by itself or when combined with PA, LR, and DV binary position relationship features performed best.
source: Among all co-dependent positional relationship features, the angular relationship feature by itself or when combined with PA, LR, and DV binary position relationship features performed best (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by feature selection experiments.

claim: Simulating missing neurons significantly increased the prediction accuracy compared to the base case that assumes all cells are present in data.
source: Compared to the base case that assumes all cells are present in data, simulating missing neurons significantly increased the prediction accuracy (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B) on experimental data.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results.

claim: CRF_ID using relative positional features performs the best compared to registration-based methods for both experimental and synthetic data.
source: Remarkably, for both experimental and synthetic data, CRF_ID using relative positional features performs the best (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by method comparison experiments.

claim: CRF_ID outperforms registration-based method across all levels of count noise and position noise in data.
source: Notably, CRF_ID outperforms registration-based method across all levels of count noise and position noise in data (Figure 2D,E; Figure 2—figure supplement 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experiments across noise levels.

claim: The accuracy of registration-based methods falls rapidly with increasing count noise levels, whereas CRF_ID is highly robust, maintaining higher accuracy even when up to 75% of cells in atlas were missing from data.
source: The accuracy of registration-based methods falls rapidly with increasing count noise levels, whereas CRF_ID is highly robust, maintaining higher accuracy even when up to 75% of cells in atlas were missing from data.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with varying count noise.

claim: Neuron positions are highly variable across individual animals.
source: Further, neuron positions being highly variable across individual animals have been shown (Yemini et al., 2021), and confirmed by our datasets as well (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is supported by citation and the authors' data.

claim: Cell positions on average can deviate from their atlas position by more than the distance to their tenth nearest neighbor.
source: Because cell positions on average can deviate from their atlas position by more than the distance to their tenth nearest neighbor (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B), we expect that this variability introduces large matching errors in registration-based methods.
evidence: This is shown by analysis of position variability.

claim: Most pair-wise relationships are preserved despite the variability of absolute positions.
source: In contrast, most pair-wise relationships are preserved despite the variability of absolute positions (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 6C,D).
evidence: This is shown by analysis of pairwise relationships.

claim: A hybrid objective function that combines registration using absolute positions with relative position features in CRF_ID framework corrupts the annotation performance.
source: Interestingly, a hybrid objective function that combines registration using absolute positions with relative position features in CRF_ID framework corrupts the annotation performance (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A), likely due to competing effects in the objective function.
evidence: This is shown by experiments with hybrid methods.

claim: Higher accuracy is achieved by positional relationship features in CRF_ID method.
source: This again highlights the fact that higher accuracy is achieved by positional relationship features in CRF_ID method.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison results.

claim: CRF_ID framework is computationally more expensive compared to CPD.
source: As expected, CRF_ID framework is computationally more expensive compared to CPD, because it optimizes both unary and pairwise potentials.
evidence: This is stated based on the computational complexity of the methods.

claim: The optimization runtime of CRF_ID framework for multi-cell calcium imaging use-case (10–50 cells in image) is on the order of 0.1–10 s on a desktop computer when full head ganglion atlas (206 cells) is used for annotation.
source: Nonetheless, the optimization runtime of CRF_ID framework for multi-cell calcium imaging use-case (10–50 cells in image) is on the order of 0.1–10 s, on a desktop computer (see Materials and methods – Runtime comparison), when full head ganglion atlas (206 cells) is used for annotation.
evidence: This is supported by runtime measurements.

claim: Using full head ganglion atlas for cell identity annotation in whole-brain imaging is important because without prior knowledge of which cells are missing in images, full atlas provides unbiased opportunity to cells in images to take any label from the atlas.
source: We emphasize that using full head ganglion atlas for cell identity annotation in whole-brain imaging is important because without prior knowledge of which cells are missing in images, full atlas provides unbiased opportunity to cells in images to take any label from the atlas.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for using full atlas.

claim: Higher accuracy compared to registration based methods combined with reasonable speeds makes CRF_ID favorable for cell annotation tasks.
source: Thus, higher accuracy compared to registration based methods combined with reasonable speeds makes CRF_ID favorable for cell annotation tasks.
evidence: This is an inference from the performance comparison.

claim: The CRF_ID framework accurately generated a candidate list for cells across all datasets (n = 21 animals) with 85% of cells having true identities within the top five labels.
source: Our framework accurately generated a candidate list for cells across all datasets (n = 21 animals); 85% of cells had true identities within the top five labels chosen by the framework.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results on gene expression data.

claim: The candidate list generated by the registration method achieved only 61% accuracy.
source: In comparison, the candidate list generated by the registration method achieved only 61% accuracy (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with registration method.

claim: The annotation framework identified neurons with high accuracy (98%, n = 35 animals) in multi-cell functional imaging experiments.
source: Indeed, our annotation framework identified neurons with high accuracy (98%, n = 35 animals).
evidence: This is supported by experimental results on multi-cell imaging.

claim: The registration method predicted identities with lower accuracy (88%) even with the small label assignment space in multi-cell functional imaging.
source: In comparison, the registration method predicted identities with lower accuracy (88%) even with the small label assignment space (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with registration method.

claim: Landmarks in the middle group and landmarks spatially distributed throughout the head performed equally well.
source: Overall, landmarks in anterior and posterior groups performed badly in predicting identities of cells in posterior and anterior groups respectively. Landmarks in the middle group and landmarks spatially distributed throughout the head performed equally (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by simulations on landmark locations.

claim: Neurons with algorithm-assigned identities demonstrate expected behavior in whole-brain imaging experiments.
source: More importantly, neurons with algorithm-assigned identities demonstrate expected behavior. For instance, we identified the sensory neuron AWC, and detected an off-response to IAA, consistent with known AWC behavior.
evidence: This is supported by the observed responses in whole-brain imaging.

claim: The predicted interneurons (e.g. AVA, RIB, and AIB) demonstrate previously known activity patterns.
source: In addition, the predicted interneurons (e.g. AVA, RIB, and AIB) also demonstrate previously known activity patterns (Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with known activity patterns and citation.

claim: Several highly entrained neurons were identified as sensory neurons known to respond to food stimuli.
source: Notably, several highly entrained neurons were identified as sensory neurons known to respond to food stimuli (Liu et al., 2019; Wakabayashi et al., 2009; Zaslaver et al., 2015; Figure 5C), some of which responded to the onset of the stimuli and some to the withdrawal of the stimuli (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by identification results and citations to known responses.

claim: Cells participating in SPC2 showed significantly higher mutual information with motion than any other component.
source: Interestingly, cells participating in SPC2 showed significantly higher mutual information with motion than any other component (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by mutual information analysis.

claim: Neurons that drive SPC2 are correlated or anti-correlated with the motion detected.
source: Examining the connection between activities of neurons that drive SPC2 and animal motion demonstrates that these neurons are indeed correlated or anti-correlated with the motion we detected (Figure 5H)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: These neurons included several command interneurons such as AVA, RIM, and motor neurons such as VA and DA.
source: notably, these neurons included several command interneurons such as AVA, RIM, and motor neurons such as VA and DA (Kato et al., 2015; Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by identification results and citation.

claim: Neurons are activated ahead of motion.
source: Cross-correlation analysis between motion and neuron activities showed that neurons are activated ahead of motion (Figure 5I)
evidence: This is supported by cross-correlation analysis.

claim: The best performing model uses relative position features in combination with color and without registration term, achieving 67.5% accuracy for the top-label prediction.
source: Notably, the best performing model uses relative position features in combination with color and without registration term (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), achieving 67.5% accuracy for the top-label prediction.
evidence: This is supported by method comparison experiments.

claim: For 85.3% of the neurons, the true identity is within the top three labels.
source: Further, for 85.3% of the neurons, the true identity is within the top three labels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results.

claim: Color contributed little to improving accuracy when using leave-one-out atlases.
source: We found that color contributed little to improving accuracy. This is because in the datasets used, the color variability in raw RGB values across animals is far greater than the position variability across animals
evidence: This is supported by comparison of results with and without color.

claim: The color variability in raw RGB values across animals is far greater than the position variability across animals.
source: This is because in the datasets used, the color variability in raw RGB values across animals is far greater than the position variability across animals; hence, the distribution of color features in the training data does not match the distribution of features in the test data.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for limited color contribution.

claim: The two-step method improves accuracy by 6% over the naïve approach.
source: The two-step method improves accuracy by 6% over the naïve approach (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of color alignment methods.

claim: Using the data-driven atlas, accuracy improved to 81% (top labels); more than 93% of the neurons have their true identities in the top three labels chosen by the model.
source: Using the data-driven atlas, accuracy improved to 81% (top labels); more than 93% of the neurons have their true identities in the top three labels chosen by the model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results with data-driven atlases.

claim: With the test data held out in atlases, the prediction accuracy of top labels was 48.8%, and the accuracy was 68.7% for top three labels for rotated animals.
source: With the test data held out in atlases, the prediction accuracy of top labels was 48.8%, and the accuracy was 68.7% for top three labels (Figure 6E ), which are reasonable for practical purposes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results on rotated animals.

claim: The CRF_ID framework is suitable for fluorescently labeled cells in 3D images for many applications.
source: Here, we demonstrated our CRF_ID framework is suitable for fluorescently labeled cells in 3D images for many applications.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the demonstrations.

claim: The CRF_ID framework is more accurate compared to existing approaches.
source: Using both ground-truth experimental data of whole-brain image stacks and synthetic data generated from an atlas, we showed that our framework is more accurate compared to existing approaches.
evidence: This is supported by comparison experiments.

claim: The CRF_ID framework significantly speeds up the cell identification compared to manual labeling while reducing bias.
source: Further, our CRF_ID framework significantly speeds up the cell identification compared to manual labeling while reducing bias.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the automated approach.

claim: The CRF_ID framework leverages intrinsic similarity, so it performs better than registration methods in handling position noise.
source: Because our framework leverages intrinsic similarity (Bronstein et al., 2007), it performs better than registration methods in handling position noise (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is supported by comparison experiments and citation.

claim: CRF_ID formulation is more accurate in handling count noise because the missing neurons do not upset the relationships among the detectable neurons.
source: Further, CRF_ID formulation is more accurate in handling count noise that is cases of missing or undetectable cells in images (Figure 2D; Figure 4C; Figure 2—figure supplement 5B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), because the missing neurons do not upset the relationships among the detectable neurons in the CRF_ID formulation while missing neurons introduce large uncertainty in registration methods.
evidence: This is supported by experiments and explanation of the method.

claim: CRF_ID method predicts identities with sufficient accuracy for different postural orientations of the worms.
source: Lastly, CRF_ID method predicts identities with sufficient accuracy for different postural orientations of the worms often seen in our microfluidic experiments.
evidence: This is supported by experiments on rotated animals.

claim: Building data-driven atlas for the CRF_ID framework requires only cheap mathematical operations, thus incorporating more data is quite simple and easily scalable.
source: Since building such data-driven atlas for our framework requires only cheap mathematical operations (Appendix 1–Extended methods S1.7), incorporating more data is quite simple and easily scalable.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method.

claim: In CRF method, atlas building is unbiased toward any image set because there is no concept of reference image.
source: In comparison, in CRF method, atlas building is unbiased toward any image set because there is no concept of reference image.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage compared to registration methods.

claim: Atlases can be built incrementally using partially or fully annotated datasets in the CRF_ID framework.
source: Another major advantage of data-driven atlases in our framework is that the atlases can be built incrementally using partially or fully annotated datasets, for example using lines that label partial and distinct subsets of cells.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method.

claim: Registration-based methods cannot build atlas from lines that label distinct subset of cells.
source: In comparison, registration-based methods cannot build atlas from lines that label distinct subset of cells. This is because registration-based methods build probabilistic spatial atlases by first establishing correspondence among cells in images and subsequently registering images.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of registration methods.

claim: CRF_ID framework can combine manually annotated data across different lines, generated by different researchers in the form of data-driven atlases.
source: Thus, in principle, CRF_ID framework can combine manually annotated data across different lines, generated by different researchers (and across labs) in the form of data-driven atlases.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the method.

claim: CRF_ID framework offers the flexibility of combining arbitrary unary features with arbitrary pairwise features for cell annotation task.
source: CRF framework offers the flexibility of combining arbitrary unary features with arbitrary pairwise features for cell annotation task.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the framework.

claim: In order to be able to utilize color information of cells in NeuroPAL for automatic annotation of cell identities, color consistency across animals needs to be maintained, either experimentally or by post hoc corrections.
source: Our experiments show that in order to be able to utilize color information of cells in NeuroPAL for automatic annotation of cell identities, color consistency across animals needs to be maintained, either experimentally or by post hoc corrections.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: The framework should be easily modifiable catering to the data demands in other organisms including features besides landmarks and spectral information such as cellular morphology and expected cellular activities.
source: Thus, framework should be easily modifiable catering to the data demands in other organisms including features besides landmarks and spectral information such as cellular morphology and expected cellular activities (e.g. calcium transients).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future applications.

claim: The framework proposed should be generally useful for many problems in model organisms such as Drosophila, zebrafish, mammalian brains.
source: Because the only inputs to our framework are segmented anatomical regions in images and positional relationships among them, information already available in data across organisms (Robie et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2019; Ronneberger et al., 2012), the framework proposed here should be generally useful for many problems in model organisms such as Drosophila (Robie et al., 2017; Vaadia et al., 2019), zebrafish (Ronneberger et al., 2012), mammalian brains (Kim et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation with citations to work in other organisms.

claim: The pipeline should also be able to work with data from other modalities including EM, live imaging, and fluorescence imaging from cleared tissues.
source: Besides fluorescence, the pipeline should also be able to work with data from other modalities including EM, live imaging, and fluorescence imaging from cleared tissues.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about applicability to other modalities.
